line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3
teaches: Do not reflexively avoid a doubled pawn — when the trade that doubles you also hands you the bishop pair and a pawn duo supporting your centre, welcome it. Judge the exchange by what you end up with, not by the tidy pawns you give up.
explains: The knight simply develops to f3. If Black grabs it, you might flinch at the doubled c-pawns — but don't: those c3 and d4 pawns brace the centre, and White keeps the strong light-squared bishop. Placing that bishop on d3 first is exactly what makes this calm reply work.

line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2 d5 e5
teaches: Advance a central pawn when the push also gains time by hitting a piece — space seized with tempo, rather than as a slow lunge, gives you a free move to get on with your plan while the opponent scrambles.
explains: The pawn to e5 grabs central space and, crucially, attacks the knight on f6, so Black has to stop and move it. That is a free tempo: White gets room for a kingside build-up while the opponent spends a move tucking the knight away.

line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2 d5 e5 Nfd7 O-O h6 a3
teaches: When an enemy bishop pins your knight and nothing forces your hand, a rook-pawn poke makes it commit — either it captures, handing you the bishop pair, or it retreats with a lasting awkwardness.
explains: The pawn to a3 pokes the bishop on b4 and forces a choice, and both answers help White: take on c3 and hand over the bishop pair with a supported centre, or drop back with a lasting headache. Ask the question — Black shoulders the answer either way.

line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2 d5 e5 Nfd7 O-O h6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 c5
teaches: In a cramped, closed structure watch for a pawn thrust that cages your own developed bishop — the space you gained can become a trap, so spot the pawn advance that hits a bishop with no retreat before it lands.
explains: Here is the catch. With c5, Black threatens to shove the pawn to c4 next, hitting the bishop on d3 which would have nowhere safe to go. It is the standard trap in this structure — White has to deal with the idea now, before getting on with the attack.

line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2 d5 e5 Nfd7 O-O h6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 c5 Qe3
teaches: Answer a threat with the move that does two jobs at once — and never trade the piece your attack depends on. A quiet queen move that guards the point and preserves your key attacker beats a developing move that invites its exchange.
explains: The queen goes to e3, and it works on two fronts: it guards the d4-pawn, and it sidesteps the bishop-to-b5 try that Black would meet with a6, forcing off White's prized light-squared bishop. The attacker stays on the board — that is the move that matters here.

line: e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Nc3 e6 Bd3 Bb4 Nf3 Nf6 Qe2 d5 e5 Nfd7 O-O h6 a3 Bxc3 bxc3 c5 Qe3 Ba6 Qf4
teaches: Reroute your queen toward the enemy king by way of a stepping-stone square — when the plan is a kingside attack, the queen's journey to its attacking post is worth the tempo, especially when the route keeps defending the centre for free.
explains: The queen swings to f4, on its way to g4 or g3 to bear down on g7 and the king. And the route costs nothing: from those squares it keeps one eye on the centre, so the attacking plan gains its ground without giving anything back.
